newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Intellectuals debate Serb issue in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Intellectuals debate Serb issue in Croatia.

text.p: With a police guard posted nearby, intellectuals ranging from wizened old socialists to contemporary human rights crusaders gathered in Croatia late last month to debate a very unpopular subject.

Despite opposition, some 160 Croats and Serbs from an isolated liberal-left intellectual community focused on bringing back more than 150,000 minority Serbs who abandoned ancestral homes to flee war or persecution after Croatia seceded in 1991.

To allow these Serbs to resettle safely as equal citizens would set an example of ethnic reconciliation to all former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia, and stabilise the new peace in the region, human rights activists say.
It would also foster a culture of civic democracy and tolerance in Croatia and further the young republic's quest for links to the European Union (EU), they maintain.

But the local chapter of the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights had to cancel its first "round table" talk about Croatia's Serb minority last April for fear of violence after hostile commentaries by the state-run media.
The forum finally assembled without incident on October 18-20 in a rented Austro-Hungarian salon in Zagreb.
To the intellectuals' chagrin, most Croatians were oblivious to the event and the powers-that-be were dismissive.
Dozens of officials from both the nationalist government and opposition parties were invited but did not show up.
"We were dissatisfied with the outcome in the sense that we ended up preaching to the already converted," said Zarko Puhovski, vice-president of Croatia's Helsinki committee.

"We were satisfied in another respect -- we made it possible for people who could not be heard for years to speak freely and publicly about a problem that must be solved for the good of Croatia's future."
A follow-up round table is to be held November 20-21 in Belgrade, capital of Serbia and the opposite pole of the Croat-Serb conflict that destroyed federal Yugoslavia.

The atmosphere at the Zagreb round table brightened just days before the forum when the Council of Europe admitted Croatia as its 40th member state. The Council sets standards of democracy and human rights and serves as the EU antechamber.

Council membership rewarded Croatia for its first steps -- taken at EU and U.S. nudging -- towards burying the hatchet with its war enemies, including a normalisation treaty with Yugoslavia and a broad amnesty for Serbs at home.

But most Croatians have long resented what they see as an inordinate preoccupation by human rights activists and the West with the rights of a minority in Croatia at the expense of the rights of a majority trampled in a war it did not start.
Around 250,000 Croats became refugees and Croatia's economy was devastated when the Yugoslav federal army intervened to back a minority Serb uprising against independence in 1991.
Many refugee Croats returned home in the past year after government troops reconquered two Serb-held enclaves.
But 80,000 still impatiently await a U.N.-supervised handover of the last enclave, Eastern Slavonia, due in 1997. Serb separatists are trying to stall the process indefinitely.

"Great efforts are always made to secure Serb rights in Croatia, while at the same time no one asks why not a single Croat has been able to return to Eastern Slavonia," Deputy Prime Minister Ivica Kostovic said during a brief, tense appearance at the round table.
He promised his government would do all it could to improve the human rights situation in Croatia but it opposed "this exaggerated internationalisation of the Serb question".

Round-table participants accused the government of saying one thing -- Serbs can come back -- and doing another -- discouraging them by posing red-tape obstacles and failing to dispense with chauvinist rhetoric that Serbs find menacing.
Some speakers, Serbs and Croats, voiced doubt that civic democracy could develop until the HDZ party, with its "unitarist nationalist" vision of Croatia, was voted out of office.

Co-moderator of the round table was Zvonimir Cicak, the Croatian Helsinki committee president whom the official media have tried to vilify as a supposed former Yugoslav secret police agent, a charge he has laughed off.

Participants in the round table included aged veterans of old Yugoslavia's World War Two partisan forces. They pleaded for a new form of the multicultural secularism that kept the peace among Yugoslavia's nations under communist rule.

That sort of sentiment elicits only denunciations of "Yugo-nostalgia" in Croatia today, the nationalist epithet for anyone supposedly bent on weakening Croatian independence, including liberal campaigners for minority rights.

"The fear of open discussion remains evident in Croatia and the only way to fight it is with dialogue," Ivo Banac, an eminent Croatian historian who teaches at Yale, said in a summary wrapping up the round table.
"We need to build a society of human dignity in Croatia. We must work to de-ethnicise Croatian society, making it one where people are judged solely on their character and merits."
